October 2009 ## **Chilean copper concentrate grades: less but not least** It is a widely discussed topic in the copper industry that concentrates grades have been decreasing. Smelters argue that the standard 30% grade is rare these days. In the latest Copper Concentrates Service report we have analysed the monthly Chilean copper concentrate grades and here we are expanding the discussion. The analysis is based on Chilean copper concentrates exports only, as there is no data available for its domestic consumption. The longest detailed data goes back to 2006. The main findings are: - There has been a negative trend in the copper concentrate grades, which is aligned with the copper ore grades. Despite the decline, the Chilean average remains above 30%. - It is the mines with higher grade concentrates that have seen a decline in the grades down towards industry average. Escondida, Los Pelambres and Collahuasi have seen the greatest declines. - In comparison to the international average – taking the Japanese consumption as an indicator – the Chilean grades remain above the average. Although, the premium (gap between Chilean and average concentrate grades) that Chilean mines used to have has been decreasing. © 2009 CRU International Limited **confidential** **October 2009** **www.crumonitor.com** ## **The ugly trend** The grade of the exported Chilean copper concentrates has been in decline from an average of 33.9% in 2006 to 30.7% in 2009 (January-July). This downward trend reflects the falling copper ore grades of the country, as we explained in the Copper South America Monthly August 2009 report. The decrease in copper concentrate grades could have also been caused by the transition in the mineralisation of the various deposits. In general, near surface mixed and secondary sulphides (chalcocite, bornita, chalcopyrite) have higher copper content than deeper primary (chalcopyrite only) ore. If these companies are mining secondary sulphides, we should expect more drops in copper grade in concentrate in the future, once they start mining the primary sulphides. ## **The usual suspects** The declines of the copper concentrate gra

des from Escondida, Los Pelambres and Collahuasi have been having the greatest impacts on the downward trend in the country’s average. Together, they exported 77% of the Chilean copper concentrates in January-July 2009. Their performances respond to their – expected or unexpected – lower copper ore grades. It is well noted that the three of them are known for their exceptionally high copper ore grades. Therefore, their declines are about not being “extraordinary” anymore, but becoming “average” operations. |Chile: exported copper

However, despite this decline, Escondida’s concentrate grades © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 6 **October 2009** www.crumonitor.com remained above the national average. A sharper fall in copper concentrate grades has occurred at Los Pelambres. Starting in early 2007, grades fell from 40.0% in February to a nadir of 29.2% in May 2008. This trend is in line with the average decline of copper ore grades. The grade of copper concentrate exported by Collahuasi decreased from a peak of 31.7% in April 2008 to 22.9% in September 2008, and has rebounded since then. There is no available information about expected ore grades or concentrate grades, but we presume that the general downward trend in Chile will continue as mines age, with a consequent impact on smelter production. ## **Mind the gap: the decreasing premium of the Chilean grades** Chilean concentrates have been losing their premium (higher content) compared to the international average. We take the Japanese consumed copper concentrate grade as a reference of international average given that it imports concentrates mainly from Chile, Peru, Indonesia, Australia and North America. # Copper production - In Chile, copper production decreased 2% y-o-y in July according to Cochilco. This is the thirteenth consecutive month of decline. The reasons are similar to those in May, April and March. Escondida alone produced 21,700t less because of lower ore grades and technical failures at its Laguna Seca SAG mill. This mill re-started on August 2nd , so Escondida’s production should increase from August. Codelco produced 14,600t more than in June 2008 mainly because of the Codelco Norte and the ramp-up at Gaby. All other operations in Chile remained at the same range. In August, according to the National Statistics Institute, copper production in Chile was 459,823t (- 7.8% y-o-y). - In Peru, copper production decreased slightly in July (less than 1% y-o-y). Cerro Verde’s copper-inconcentrates production declined by 20% to 17,400t; partly offset by the ramp-up at Cerro Corona (3,300t more than in July 2008). Cuajone’s copper-in-concentrates production increased by 25% to 11,500t and offsets minor declines in other mines. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 6 **October 2009** **www.crumonitor.com** |**Jul**
